title: Microfluidic-based high-precision fluorescence microscopy of lipid packing in membrane vesicles
author: Zhurgenbayeva, Otrin, et al.

steps.title: Prepare 300 mM sucrose solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 513.4 mg sucrose crystals in 5 mL Milli‑Q water to obtain a 300 mM sucrose solution (S1). Prepare fresh and store at 21 °C–23 °C for no more than 24 h.

steps.title: Prepare isotonic sucrose‑glucose solution
steps.instruction: In a 5 mL tube combine 479.2 mg sucrose (280 mM) and 18.0 mg glucose (20 mM) with Milli‑Q water to a final volume of 5 mL (solution S2). Prepare fresh and store at 21 °C–23 °C for no more than 24 h.

steps.title: Prepare 10 mg/mL BSA solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 100 mg BSA powder in 10 mL Milli‑Q water to obtain a 10 mg/mL BSA solution. Allow any foam to settle before use. Store at 4 °C for up to 7 days.

steps.title: Prepare lipid stock solutions
steps.instruction: Rinse glass vials sequentially with Milli‑Q water, pure ethanol, and chloroform; blow‑dry with filtered compressed air between washes. Dissolve cholesterol powder in chloroform to 25 mg/mL. POPC is supplied pre‑dissolved in chloroform at 25 mg/mL. Store stocks in amber screw‑cap vials at –20 °C under argon or nitrogen, sealing with PTFE tape and parafilm.

steps.title: Make lipid mixtures L1 and L2
steps.instruction: In clean vials prepare two 1 mL lipid mixtures in chloroform:

substeps.instruction: L1 (pure POPC, 4 mM or 3.04 mg/mL): pipette 121.6 µL POPC stock and add chloroform to 1 mL total.
L2 (POPC:cholesterol 70:30, 3.86 mM or 2.5 mg/mL): pipette 82 µL POPC stock and 18 µL cholesterol stock, then add chloroform to 1 mL total.

steps.title: Mix and degas PDMS
steps.instruction: Combine silicone elastomer base and curing agent in a 10:1 mass ratio (e.g., 70 g base + 7 g curing agent) in a plastic weighing bowl. Mix thoroughly with a wooden stick until homogeneous. Degas the mixture in a vacuum desiccator, then slowly pour onto the wafer, degassing again if bubbles remain near features.

steps.title: Cast, cure, and cut PDMS chip
steps.instruction: Place the wafer with poured PDMS in an oven at 80 °C for 1 h. Allow the PDMS block to cool to 21 °C–23 °C. Cut the cured PDMS into individual chips with a scalpel.

steps.title: Punch inlet and outlet ports
steps.instruction: Place each PDMS chip with the microchannel side up and punch inlet and outlet holes using biopsy punches. Use a 1.5 mm diameter punch for the inlet and a 1.0 mm punch for the outlet. Cover the channel surface with invisible tape to avoid dust contamination.

steps.title: Clean and plasma‑activate coverslip
steps.instruction: Clean both sides of a glass coverslip with detergent for ~20 s, rinse sequentially with Milli‑Q water, 70 % ethanol, and Milli‑Q water again, then blow‑dry with filtered compressed air (alternatively soak in 2 % SDS for ≥2 h, rinse, and blow‑dry). Place the chip and coverslip in a plasma cleaner (microchannel side up) and treat both surfaces for 60 s at ~1 mbar.

steps.title: Bond PDMS chip to coverslip and bake
steps.instruction: Immediately after plasma treatment, align the PDMS block (microchannel side down) onto the coverslip, press gently to remove air bubbles, and ensure full contact. Visually inspect critical structures (posts, traps). Place the assembled chip in an oven at 80 °C for 1 h (or leave at 21 °C–23 °C for 12–16 h) to complete bonding.

steps.title: Assemble inlet/outlet reservoirs
steps.instruction: Cut a 200 µL and a 1000 µL pipette tip to ~2 cm length. Insert the 1000 µL tip into the 1.5 mm inlet and the 200 µL tip into the 1.0 mm outlet until both tips touch the coverslip base. Adjust reservoir height to fit microscope stage clearance.

steps.title: Coat channels with BSA and centrifuge
steps.instruction: Add 50 µL BSA solution to the inlet reservoir in one continuous push to avoid air bubbles. Place the chip in a centrifuge with appropriate holders, balance with another chip, and centrifuge at 900 × g for 10 min. Confirm that the BSA solution equilibrates in both reservoirs after spinning.

steps.title: Rinse and pre‑fill Hamilton syringe with S2
steps.instruction: Rinse a 1 mL gastight Hamilton syringe with isopropanol followed by Milli‑Q water and blow‑dry. Fill the syringe with isotonic sucrose‑glucose solution (S2): first load 0.2 mL to eliminate bubbles, then continue filling to 1 mL total. This ensures bubble‑free loading for stable flow.

steps.title: Load tubing and connect to chip
steps.instruction: Connect tubing to the syringe using a PEEK‑luer adapter (pre‑assembled with a metal connector at the chip end). Fill the tubing with S2 until the metal connector end is reached, then continue filling until the total volume in the tubing is 0.8 mL, leaving 0.2 mL of S2 in the syringe. Remove the outlet reservoir, insert the metal tubing connector into the outlet port until it touches the coverslip, and ensure a small droplet remains at the connector tip to maintain a water‑to‑water interface.

steps.title: Set up and test syringe pump
steps.instruction: Turn on the Cetoni Base pump and launch the Cetoni Elements software. Click “Connect to device” (plug icon). Reconfigure syringe settings: select syringe type “Glass”, volume “1 mL”, and click “Apply syringe”. Test the pump by clicking the “Refill syringe” icon and confirming plunger movement, then click “Stop dosing”. Set the syringe level to ~200 µL to secure its position.

steps.title: Mount syringe and chip on microscope stage
steps.instruction: Mount the syringe onto the pump and secure it with two fixative bolts, attaching the appropriate plunger holder. Place the assembled chip (with inlet/outlet reservoirs) on the microscope stage and secure both chip and syringe using fixation clamps.

steps.title: Acquire confocal images of trapped GUVs
steps.instruction: Transfer the assembled microfluidic unit onto the confocal microscope stage. Use the appropriate objective (e.g., Olympus UPlanXApo 20×/0.8 air) and set two‑channel detection (ordered and disordered wavelength ranges) to capture GP‑compatible images of GUVs trapped in the microfluidic channels.

steps.title: Analyze GP values in Fiji
steps.instruction: Open Fiji, load the Fluidity Calculator macro via More Tools → (double‑arrow) → Fluidity Calculator. Open the acquired two‑channel image (e.g., .msr) ensuring both channels are selected in the Bio‑Formats Series Options window. Merge the channels (Image → Color → Merge Channels) assigning Channel 1 to the ordered (Io) and Channel 2 to the disordered (Id) emission. Launch the Fluidity Calculator, confirm the channel assignments, set an intensity threshold to exclude background, and press OK to run the analysis. The macro outputs a pseudocolored GP map, a GP histogram, and statistics (mean, median, standard deviation). Keep threshold settings consistent across datasets.

description: Membrane lipid packing is one of the key determinants of membrane organization. Fluorescence-based generalized polarization (GP) microscopy employing polarity-sensitive dyes provides a sensitive measure of lipid packing, but achieving precise quantification is often hindered by sample drift of e.g., membrane vesicles such as giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) in aqueous environments. Conventional ways to tackle the issue of sample drifts involve utilizing either a sticky surface from a dried thin layer of bovine serum albumin (BSA) or streptavidin-biotin affinities to immobilize GUVs onto the coverslip surface. Nevertheless, these endeavors only result in wobbly GUVs, and could potentially alter local membrane compositions, induce shape transformations, as well as eventually lead to inaccurate analysis on lipid packing.3,4,5 To address these limitations, this protocol utilizes polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)-based microfluidic chips to immobilize GUVs without perturbing their integrity. This setup enables stable two-channel confocal GP imaging of GUV membranes by employing polarity-sensitive solvatochromic dyes such as Nile Red derivatives like NR12A or classical Laurdan probes. These dyes’ emission spectra shifts in response to changes in membrane lipid packing order, exhibiting a red shift in less packed and thus more disordered membrane environments and a blue shift in more ordered environments.6 Such environment-sensitive probes provide robust optical readouts of membrane biophysical properties like lipid packing and order,7 membrane viscosity,8 and membrane tension,9 which are all inter-connected. Using these environment-sensitive probes, membrane lipid packing or order is commonly quantified using the GP parameter, which is usually calculated from intensities collected in two spectral channels, one at a shorter more blueish and one at a longer more reddish wavelength-range. Specifically, Io (ordered) and Id (disordered) refer to the fluorescence intensities measure
